articles.title: US, China to discuss AI safety risks, cooperation on monitoring AI-directed cyberattacks
articles.body:
The US and China are gearing up to discuss AI safety risks during a dialogue planned for mid-September, two sources briefed on the discussions told Reuters, as rapidly advancing frontier AI capabilities reach a global tipping point.
The talks, the first official bilateral discussions devoted exclusively to AI between the US and China since US President Donald Trump took office for a second time, will be led by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the US side, the sources, who were briefed on the planning, said on condition of anonymity.
Reuters is reporting the tentative mid-September period for the first time. A White House official said, "There is currently no planned AI-related meeting in mid-September." Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are due to meet on September 24 during a summit in Washington.
The US wants to discuss cooperation on monitoring AI-directed cyberattacks, and has floated a proposal to ask US and Chinese AI labs to "police themselves" and share information to prevent AI-linked cyberattacks, one of the sources said on condition of anonymity.
Autonomous AI agent incidents add urgency to superpowers' talks
Nearly 700 rogue AI agents built on OpenAI models hacked AI startup Hugging Face in July and attempted to cover their tracks by forging logs, OpenAI and cybersecurity researchers said last week, underscoring the risks of coordinated agent swarms acting autonomously for months undetected by humans.
A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, Reuters exclusively reported on Friday.
"The talks between the two AI superpowers are coming at the most critical juncture," said Paul Triolo, a partner at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group. "It is now or never."
Washington is also worried about the potential for a future Chinese Mythos-level model with capabilities to conduct cyberattacks, and wants to bring up alleged Chinese distillation of proprietary US AI models, the source said.
US tech firm Anthropic is the developer of Mythos.
In June, top White House science and tech advisor Michael Kratsios accused China's Moonshot AI of stealing from Anthropic's AI model Fable to help create its K3 release, saying the Chinese company distilled Anthropic's model.
Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using output from larger, more expensive ones as part of an effort to lower the costs of training a powerful new AI tool.
Reuters is reporting details of the upcoming talks' proposed agenda for the first time.
On the Chinese side, the talks could be led by Vice Premier He Lifeng, Bessent's protocol counterpart, but alternatives such as China's No. 7 official Ding Xuexiang may be considered, according to the second source, who also spoke on condition of anonymity.
Ding, a confidant of Xi and a member of the ruling Communist Party's powerful seven-person Politburo Standing Committee, coordinates China's technology, AI and semiconductor policies.
Reuters could not determine the location or identity of other participants, though Kratsios and China's science and technology minister, Yin Hejun, could attend the talks, the second source added.
The final agenda and participants remain in flux, the sources cautioned.
The White House declined to comment on the AI talks. The State Department did not respond to a request for comment. China's foreign, science and industry ministries, as well as the National Development and Reform Commission and cyberspace regulator, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
On Tuesday, Kratsios told reporters in North Carolina that he had a "great" meeting with Yin on the sidelines of a G20 innovation summit in the US this week. Bessent said he had "limited" exchanges on AI with Chinese officials at this week's G20 finance meeting.
The US urged G20 members to take a hands-off approach to AI regulation and avoid creating rules for the technology at the same innovation summit. China signed the Carolina Principles, an agreement aimed at discouraging the development of AI-specific regulations, in a rare show of tech alignment with the US
Kratsios' office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Talks emphasized as high importance
Chinese officials have repeatedly stressed the importance of the AI talks in preparatory meetings with US counterparts, and view them as a major deliverable of the US-China leaders' summit, according to the two sources and another one familiar with the matter. Reuters is reporting this development for the first time.
In the past week, China's cyberspace regulator publicly warned about "extreme AI loss of control risks" and a state media-affiliated blog criticized Anthropic, emphasizing that any limits on frontier AI should apply equally to Chinese and US models. Chinese firms have in recent months unveiled what they describe as Mythos-like products.
Former Microsoft executive Craig Mundie has emerged as an important go-between behind the scenes, sounding out Chinese counterparts on US proposals for the AI dialog, the source said. Mundie is co-chair of the unofficial US-China Track II AI dialog channel.
Reuters reported last month that Microsoft had cultivated a relationship with Beijing that was among the deepest of any foreign technology company operating in China.
Both sides also discussed AI guardrails at a Track 1.5 dialog in Beijing last week, former Australian Prime Minister Kevin Rudd, a participant, wrote on social media.
In June, Trump signed an AI executive order setting up a voluntary framework for pre-release cybersecurity reviews of frontier AI models, but the US has not released the criteria for these reviews.
Meanwhile, employees at top US AI labs including Anthropic and OpenAI have called for "pacing the frontier" to manage the global risks of advanced AI.
"The Chinese side has expressed concern around whether the US has sufficient regulation around the most advanced AI models. Both sides are motivated to make sure they can manage a cross-border crisis effectively," said Scott Singer, co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
While outcomes are likely to be limited, opening a channel where both sides could share observations and jointly monitor AI safety incidents would be an important starting point, said Samm Sacks, a senior fellow at New America, a US policy think tank.
"We are at a tipping point where frontier agents can cause massive damage when unmonitored. Both the US and China are vulnerable. This is beyond geopolitical rivalry," Sacks added.
"The US and China have to come together in some form, or we're both going to lose."

articles.title: Sub-forums of Asia-Pacific Media Forum held in S China's Guangdong
articles.body:
Guests attend the Asia-Pacific Media Forum Shenzhen Sub-forum in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Sept. 4, 2026.
The Asia-Pacific Media Forum will open on Saturday in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, as the country hosts a series of events under the 2026 APEC "China Year."
Multiple outcomes are expected to be unveiled at the forum, under the theme of "Building a Path to Shared Prosperity for the Asia-Pacific Community: Media Consensus and Action."
From Sept. 3 to 4, the forum held four sub-forums in Guangzhou, Dongguan, Zhuhai, and Shenzhen in Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Dai Mingxuan)

articles.title: Stranded people rescued following torrential rains in Putian City, SE China's Fujian
articles.body:
Rescuers evacuate stranded people at the Hualin economic development zone in Putian City, southeast China's Fujian Province, Sept. 4, 2026. Continuous torrential rains led to severe waterlogging at the Hualin economic development zone in Putian. articles.title: From Saul's failure to David's reckoning, 'Human Kingship' examines the dangers of power - review
articles.body:
Nathan the prophet walks into David’s palace, tells the king to his face that he has murdered a man and taken his wife, and walks out again, leaving him on the throne. Punishment follows, and it is severe. The child dies. The sword, David is told, will never depart from his house. But nothing touches his hold on the office, because no tribunal stands over him and no procedure exists to remove him. The Torah never wrote one.
Instead, it supplies a list of prohibitions.
The king may not keep many horses, may not take many wives, and may not amass silver and gold to excess.
On what the job consists of, and on what is to be done if the man holding it fails, Deuteronomy says nothing at all.
Human Kingship: Studies in the Book of Samuel works that silence for all its worth. It calls itself a book of studies rather than a commentary and means it, running no continuous line and asking that you reread the Book of Samuel first. Forty years of teaching Samuel stand behind it, most of them at Drisha, the New York institute he founded in 1979, when a house of study organized around women learning Talmud was close to unheard of.
Nobody in the book is ever put out of office.
Eli, the priest at Shiloh whose two sons were seizing the people’s offerings by force, is told his house is finished and dies on the job.
Samuel tells Saul at Gilgal, after Saul offers a sacrifice without waiting for him, that his dynasty is over, and Saul reigns for years afterward.
Punishment lands on sons and houses, never on tenure, which is why Rabbi Silber’s book asks the question it does.
With no procedure to stop a king, what stands between the office and disaster?
If no procedure exists to stop a king, the only thing between the office and disaster is whether the man in it still knows what he is. The standard he measures them against is fixed and biblical: tzedek u’mishpat, justice and righteousness.
God tells Samuel three times to heed the people, and Samuel heeds, though he disagrees. Rabbi Silber fences the criticism before he makes it, noting that Samuel “is depicted in a critical light when the issue of monarchy comes to the fore” and not otherwise. On that question, what he shows is a prophet who would not let the arrangement work.
Asked to describe how a king behaves, Samuel produces a catalog of confiscation meant to talk the nation out of it. He also has an interest he never discloses, since the elders came to him because his own sons were on the take from the bench, and what stung him was not the comparison to other nations but the word “judge.” Nobody ever asks him about any of it.
On the day of his coronation, the lot falls to Saul, and he cannot be found. Of the explanations Rabbi Silber weighs for the hiding place, the one that stays is evasion, the refusal to stand and answer, for which he reaches back to Eden and Adam, the first man, hiding in the garden.
Saul is the man the system breaks, and the book never lets you forget he did not ask for it. Whether a man can hold the office and still understand himself as mortal and accountable and no more than that is the question the whole book is asking.
In a chapter where Rabbi Silber’s method is most worth watching, at Ein Gedi, Saul walks into a cave alone, unaware that the men hunting him are farther inside, and comes out again with only a piece missing from his robe. Ralbag, the French Provençal commentator Levi ben Gershon, thought David had swung to kill Saul and missed. Abrabanel, writing after the Spanish expulsion, took the remorse afterward as a scruple so fine that damaging the royal garment registered as an attack on the crown.
Rabbi Silber will have neither. David is the best soldier in the book; his target is unarmed in an enclosed space, and men like that do not miss. He sends the reader instead back to the moment Saul tore Samuel’s cloak and was told the kingdom had been torn away in the same motion.
A king’s garments are his standing, so cutting the corner off Saul’s cloak is a public statement that its owner no longer reigns. That is exactly the permission David’s men were waiting for. In this reading, the scene is not about mercy. David is telling them they may finish it themselves, and he calls them back only when he grasps what he has just authorized.
Not every link holds that well.
A book built on accumulation asks you to accept each reading before the next one lands, and while the cloak is unanswerable, others rest on shared letters or a repeated verb and buckle under the weight. The absence of an index does not help in a book that works by sending you to another chapter.
None of which makes it the wrong book, only the wrong first one. This is not a volume for a reader meeting Samuel for the first time and does not pretend to be. It is for someone who has already read the book and came away suspecting there was a great deal in it he had walked past.
The answer, when it comes, is a sentence at a threshing floor, and Rabbi Silber gives the last quarter of the book to reading it against Abraham. Seeing the angel striking down his people, David tells God the guilt is his alone and asks that the blow fall on him instead. Nothing in the book compels him to say it.
Someone once asked for such a man, before there was an office to ask about. The book opens with a barren woman at Shiloh, praying in the same corrupted sanctuary Eli’s sons were running, and she ends her prayer by asking God to give strength to a king who does not yet exist. Hannah wanted justice to have someone to carry it.
Rabbi Silber’s closing position is that it remains possible, and it has not been claimed again since.
HUMAN KINGSHIP: STUDIES IN THE BOOK OF SAMUEL 
By Rabbi David Silber 
Translated by Ilana Kurshan 
Koren/Maggid Books 
228 pages; $30

articles.title: Land section of Jintang undersea tunnel achieves full breakthrough in E China's Zhejiang
articles.body:
A construction worker works at the entrance of the Jintang undersea tunnel, east China's Zhejiang Province, Sept. 4, 2026. The 7.83-km land section of the 16.18-km Jintang undersea tunnel achieved full breakthrough on Friday. The tunnel is an important facility for the Yongzhou (Ningbo-Zhoushan) high-speed railway, and is designed as a single-bore, double-track tunnel for speeds of up to 250 km per hour. (Xinhua/Xu Yu)
